vw.why: Urdu, Hindi and Punjabi have one sound between V and W, so "very" and "wary", "vest" and "west" sound the same. Interviewers hear it constantly in words like version, value, service and web.
vw.how: V: upper teeth lightly touch your lower lip, then buzz — "vvv". W: round your lips like "oo", teeth do NOT touch. Put a finger on your lip: V vibrates, W doesn't.
lines: We validate every value before we save a new version.
Our web view works well with virtual servers.
I was very involved in the service worker work.

th.why: Many South Asian speakers say "th" as a soft T or D, so "three" sounds like "tree" and "they" like "day". It's very common in "the", "with", "method", "thread".
th.how: Put the tip of your tongue lightly between your teeth and push air out. For "think, three, method" just air (no voice). For "the, they, with" add voice (buzz).
lines: The third thread handles authentication for these methods.
I think throughput matters more than theory here.
We tested it with and without the cache.

sc.t: S at the start (no extra vowel)
sc.why: Urdu speakers often add a small vowel before S-clusters — "iskool", "istack", "isprint". Punjabi speakers add one inside — "sakool". It makes tech words sound unclear.
sc.how: Start with a long hiss "sss" and slide straight into the next sound: "sss-tack", "sss-kool". No "i" before, no "a" between.
lines: Our stack stores the schema in a script.
I split the sprint into small stories.
Strong skills in structured queries and scaling.

ed.why: Dropping final consonants ("ask" for "asked", "test" for "tests") makes past experience sound like the present — and interviewers ask about the past.
ed.how: -ed sounds like /t/ after voiceless sounds (asked, fixed, cached), /d/ after voiced sounds (deployed, handled), and /id/ after t or d (tested, loaded). Finish the last sound clearly; don't add a vowel after it.
lines: I asked, tested and fixed the failed tasks.
We cached the results and indexed the requests.
Last year I worked on three projects and deployed them weekly.

vow.why: Mixing "ship/sheep" or "full/fool" changes meaning; "build" and "field" are common tech examples.
vow.how: Long ee: smile and hold it (sheep, feel, field). Short i: relaxed and quick (ship, fill, build). Long oo: round and hold (fool, pool); short u: relaxed (full, pull).
lines: We build the feature and then feed the field.
Please leave the live server alone.
Keep the list short and the lead time low.

st.why: English is stress-timed: one syllable in each word is louder and longer. Pakistani English tends to be syllable-timed (every syllable equal), which makes long tech words harder to catch.
st.how: Say the CAPITAL syllable louder, longer and a little higher. Make the other syllables short, almost "uh".
lines: I was responsible for the architecture and the development environment.
We improved performance with a more efficient algorithm.

tech.why: Saying these the standard way sounds instantly more senior.
tech.how: Tap 🔊 to hear it, then say it. The spelling in grey shows how it sounds.

fixes: I am having five years of experience.
I have five years of experience.
Use the simple present for states: have, know, understand.
I am working here since 2021.
I have been working here since 2021.
Since/for with an ongoing action → present perfect continuous.
I have worked there since three years.
I worked there for three years.
"for" + a period; "since" + a starting point.
Let us discuss about the design.
Let us discuss the design.
"discuss" already means "talk about".
I will revert back to you.
I will get back to you.
"revert" means go back to an earlier state; in interviews say "get back to you".
Please do the needful.
Please take care of it.
Sounds outdated to international teams.
Myself Ahmed, I am from Lahore.
I'm Ahmed, and I'm from Lahore.
"Myself" can't start a sentence.
I passed out in 2020.
I graduated in 2020.
"Passed out" means fainted in international English.
I did my graduation from UET.
I graduated from UET.
Shorter and natural.
Can you explain me the requirement?
Can you explain the requirement to me?
explain something TO someone.
One of my friend helped.
One of my friends helped.
"one of" + plural.
I didn't went there.
I didn't go there.
After did/didn't use the base verb.
We need to cope up with the load.
We need to cope with the load.
No "up".
Kindly tell me the timings.
Could you tell me the time?
"Kindly" in every sentence sounds formal; "timings" → "time/schedule".
Yes sir, yes sir, correct sir.
Yes, that's right.
Too many "sir"s sound nervous; use names or nothing.
Basically, actually, I basically worked on APIs.
I worked on APIs.
Fillers make you sound unsure. Pause silently instead.

ph: Top up — one more short sniff
Long, slow exhale through your mouth
